papers.title: A live online exercise program for older adults improves depression and life-space mobility: A mixed-methods pilot randomized controlled trial
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2024, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The aim was to determine the preliminary effectiveness of a live online exercise program on older adults' physical activity levels, compared with a waitlist control group. Older adults have described numerous barriers to participating in physical activity and exercise.
papers.methodology: A pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods RCT of community-dwelling older adults aged 65 to 80 in Hamilton, Ontario. Measures included an accelerometer and the Geriatric Depression Scale Short Form. Interviews were semi-structured and thematically analyzed. Analysis used a two-way repeated measures ANOVA.
papers.theory: The study was guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement for pilot and feasibility trials.
papers.results: The ACTIVE group decreased on the Geriatric Depression Scale (interaction p = 0.012) and increased on life-space mobility (interaction p = 0.014). No between-group differences for daily steps and daily active energy expenditure, anxiety, loneliness, or nutrition risk. Attendance was 97%. Participants were satisfied or very satisfied 98% of the time. Five themes were identified.
papers.discussion: The authors report that the program did not affect habitual physical activity but reduced depressive symptoms, improved life-space mobility, and had excellent adherence and acceptability. They describe online exercise programs as viable service-delivery options, particularly when in-person programming is unavailable. They suggest the program has the potential to support synchronous exercise programs at home.
papers.limitations: The authors cite the small sample size, an underpowered pilot, and no blinding of assessors or participants. Only English-speaking people with home internet access were included. Future work should include marginalized populations, multi-component interventions, and synchronous group programs on functional assessments.

papers.title: Effectiveness of exercise-based rehabilitation for depressive symptoms, anxiety, and health-related quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The review aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise on depressive symptoms, anxiety and health-related quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis. The authors noted that whether exercise improves these outcomes remains uncertain.
papers.methodology: Conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and EBSCOhost from inception to 26 November 2025. Included randomized controlled trials of structured exercise against non-exercise controls. Random-effects meta-analyses used Hedges’ g; RoB 2 and GRADE were applied.
papers.results: Exercise was associated with lower depressive symptom scores (11 trials, 685 participants; standardized mean difference −0.49; 95% confidence interval −0.70 to −0.28; P < 0.001). Anxiety scores were lower (standardized mean difference −0.45). Quality of life improved (Hedges’ g standardized mean difference 0.45; P = 0.001). No significant subgroup difference between conventional and mind-body exercise for each outcome.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that structured exercise was associated with reductions in depressive symptoms and anxiety, and improved health-related quality of life. They suggest exercise may provide benefits as an adjunct to standard care, but evidence is insufficient to identify the most effective modality. Exercise should be integrated into care, not substituted for pharmacologic or formal mental-health care.
papers.limitations: The authors cite small trials that varied in interventions, comparators and instruments, self-reported outcomes, and mostly immediate post-intervention data, so durability is uncertain. The number of studies per outcome was limited. English-only inclusion may have introduced language bias. Future trials should prespecify outcomes, enroll larger samples, include longer follow-up, and measure mediators such as self-efficacy and fear of movement.

Low-certainty evidence suggested reductions in anxiety (7 trials, 403 participants; standardized mean difference, −0.45; 95% confidence interval, −0.65 to −0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%) and improvements in quality of life or health-related quality of life (7 trials, 564 participants; Hedges’ g standardized mean difference, 0.45; 95% confidence interval, 0.18 to 0.71; P = 0.001; I² = 50%).

papers.introduction: The protocol aims to guide a future review of the effects of aerobic exercise on reducing depression levels in adults. The authors note that many existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses have methodological limitations that prevent definitive conclusions.
papers.methodology: A protocol for a systematic review with meta-analysis of aerobic exercise for depression in adults, following PRISMA-P 2020. Searches will cover BVS, Cochrane library, Embase, Epistemonikos, PubMed and SPORTDiscus. Risk of bias will be assessed with RoB 2.0 and certainty with GRADE.
papers.results: The paper is a protocol and reports no results.
papers.discussion: The authors expect the review to identify the effective dose-response to reduce depression levels and to provide an understanding of the mechanisms through which aerobic exercise influences depression. They also expect it to specify which intensities, frequencies and durations produce the most favorable outcomes.
papers.limitations: The authors anticipate limitations including small sample sizes, a lack of clarity about mechanisms, variation in intensity protocols, and high heterogeneity among studies. A narrative synthesis will discuss research gaps for future investigations.

papers.title: Physical activity and depressive symptoms among college students: positive mental health as a mediator
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Psychology (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study aims to explore whether positive mental health mediates the link between physical activity and depressive symptoms. It notes that the psychological mechanisms through which physical activity exerts its effects are a key issue for research.
papers.methodology: A cross-sectional online survey of 3,140 Chinese college students aged 18–27 years was conducted between May and June 2025 using convenience sampling. Measures: Physical Activity Rank Scale-3 (PARS-3), Positive Mental Health Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Analysis: mediation analysis, with indirect effects tested by bias-corrected bootstrap using 5,000 resamples.
papers.theory: The study is anchored in Self-Determination Theory, which identifies autonomy, competence and relatedness as three innate psychological needs.
papers.results: The indirect effect through positive mental health was significant, ab = −0.007, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.004]. The direct effect became non-significant, c’ = −0.008, p = 0.080. The total effect was significant, c = −0.015, p < 0.01. Physical activity showed a positive association with positive mental health, a = 0.027, p < 0.001.
papers.discussion: The authors present positive mental health as a useful conceptual focus for future research and describe the indirect effect as small and of limited clinical relevance at the individual level. They recommend that colleges develop conducive spaces and engaging sports programs, provide mental health education courses, and that professionals consider physical activity prescriptions for students needing support.
papers.limitations: The cross-sectional design prevents confirmation of causal sequences, self-reported positive mental health may not fully capture culturally distinct well-being, PARS-3 internal consistency was modest (α = 0.634), and convenience sampling limits generalizability. Future work should use longitudinal designs, replicate findings in probabilistically sampled populations, and prioritize cross-cultural validation.

papers.title: A Pilot Cross-Sectional Study on the Level of Depression and Physical Activity among Students in Poland and Portugal in the Second Year of the COVID-19 Pandemic
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2023, Medicine (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The aim was a preliminary assessment of depression rates, physical activity levels and the relationship between them among Polish and Portuguese students. Poland had one of the longest education lockdowns in Europe, so the researchers compared the two countries.
papers.methodology: An online cross-sectional survey of 398 students aged 17 to 26 from Poland (229) and Portugal (169) was conducted in October 2022. Measures: Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and an abbreviated International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ). Analysis: Mann–Whitney, chi-square, Spearman's rank correlation and Kruskal–Wallis tests.
papers.results: No statistically significant difference in BDI values between the two countries was found, neither for men nor for women. Moderate depression affected 20–35% of respondents. Among Portuguese women, no statistically significant correlation between activity and depression was found. In both countries, more frequent walking had the strongest effect on reducing BDI (in Poland, rS = −0.42; in Portugal, rS = −0.28).
papers.discussion: The authors call the prevalence of moderate depression alarming and report that pilot studies showed not many statistically significant differences in depression and physical activity levels between Polish and Portuguese students. They call for further research on physical activity and mental health in different populations, to adjust the optimal level of physical activity.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the cross-sectional nature of the study does not provide robust and causal evidence, that the sample was small and the findings preliminary, that the online survey format leaves respondents' identity unknown, and that self-report questionnaires may bias responses. Future studies should target a larger sample and use more objective methods to assess the parameters studied.

papers.title: Experiences of exercise and mental well-being among psychiatric inpatients: a qualitative study
papers.introduction: The aim was to explore how psychiatric inpatients experience exercise, particularly regarding their mental well-being. The authors note that research on inpatients remains limited, as most existing studies focus on outpatients.
papers.methodology: A qualitative study of a purposive sample of eight inpatients with serious mental health disorders who had participated in individualized exercise sessions: five men and three women, mean age 53.9. Open-ended, semi-structured telephone interviews, transcribed verbatim, were analysed with reflexive thematic analysis, at one hospital in Norway.
papers.results: Four themes were identified: follow-up support, symptom reduction, sense of mastery and activation during hospitalization. Participants reported immediate improvements in mood and perceived mental well-being following exercise. The exercise physiologist was described as a crucial source of motivation and support. Some participants were uncertain about effects on sleep or energy.
papers.discussion: The authors state that exercise had a positive role in participants’ perceived mental state, and that support and follow-up are key to implementing exercise interventions for inpatients. They state that the results may suggest more inpatients should be given the opportunity to exercise regularly, while stressing that the findings reflect subjective experiences rather than treatment efficacy or causal effects.
papers.limitations: The authors note a small sample of eight, limited transferability, possible selection and social desirability bias from recruitment by the exercise physiologist, and no comparator, which makes perceived exercise effects difficult to distinguish from other treatment. Telephone interviews limited access to non-verbal cues. Future studies should include a broader, more diverse sample, and further research is needed to examine efficacy.

papers.title: Improvements in physical activity and depression symptoms: an observational study of users of a multi-modal digital mental health platform
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Biomedical Engineering; 3 other categories also Q1; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The authors examined depression and physical activity in real-world employees with access to a multi-modal digital mental health platform. They note a paucity of data on its impact on different areas of health and well-being.
papers.methodology: Prospective, observational study with online surveys at baseline and follow-up. Adults aged 18 or older in the United States who had registered for an employer-sponsored, multi-modal digital mental health benefits platform. Conducted September 2021 to May 2022; 755 adults at baseline. Measures: IPAQ-Short Form and PHQ-9. Paired t-tests and correlations.
papers.results: Of 755 adults at baseline, 47.3% were deemed underactive. Physical activity was negatively correlated with baseline PHQ-9 scores (r = −.19, p < .001). Participants screening positive at baseline reported a decrease of 4.88 points on the PHQ-9, a statistically significant 35% reduction. Underactive participants increased MVPA by 60.33 min/week, a 117% increase. Active participants reported no significant change; 78.4% stayed active.
papers.discussion: The authors state that digital, remotely delivered interventions may be particularly beneficial for underactive adults seeking mental health support or aiming to increase physical activity. They also state that employer-sponsored platforms offering integrated mental and physical health resources may create a more supportive environment for sustaining health behaviors.
papers.limitations: They were unable to determine the temporal sequence of changes, and an experimental design is needed to test causality. The single-item impact measure has yet to be validated. They did not examine industry sector. Completers had more White-identifying participants, and employer-gated access limits generalizability. Future investigations should use a longer-term follow-up, perhaps 6 or 12 months.

papers.methodology: Planned systematic and meta-analytic review of RCTs of chronic exercise in older adults with a mean age of 60 years or above. Electronic databases will be searched from inception. Comorbidities or physical fitness level still require further research to understand their influence.
